projects.title: Guest Pass
projects.problem: Temporary door access for LenelS2's Elements platform. Hosts create a pass, guests unlock from their phone, and credentials expire automatically.

caseStudy.title: Overview
paragraphs: Guest Pass is a feature I designed for Elements, LenelS2's cloud access control platform, during my co-op in 2021.

The host sets when the pass starts and ends, picks which door readers the guest can reach, and shares a link. The guest opens it on their phone and taps unlock. When the window closes, the pass deletes itself.
It released in Q4 2021. The feature is included in sales demonstrations and has generated ongoing requests for additional capability.

caseStudy.title: Who is LenelS2?
paragraphs: LenelS2 develops physical security software for access control, video, and mobile credentials. Elements is their cloud platform for managing badge readers and cameras across a facility.

caseStudy.title: What is Elements?
paragraphs: Elements is LenelS2's SaaS platform for access control and video management. Companies use it to monitor facilities with cameras and badge readers.

caseStudy.title: Problem
paragraphs: Before Guest Pass, granting visitor access in Elements required creating a full person record, normally reserved for employees, and manually revoking it later.
Customers needed a way to grant temporary visitors access without creating permanent credentials or coordinating access through the lobby.

caseStudy.title: Solution
paragraphs: Create a temporary guest pass that activates and deletes itself according to the host's settings.

caseStudy.title: Users
bullets: A person who works at a company and is inviting a guest to their company’s facility (e.g., a hiring manager inviting someone for an interview, or management inviting a business client for a meeting)
A guest who was invited to the company’s facility

subsections.title: Issuing a Guest Pass
bullets: Users need to be able to add guest passes and send them themselves as they are responsible for the guest
Optional start/end date
Assign door readers to the guest pass
A method to share the guest pass
An email template for when a guest pass is shared
The ability to update a guest pass

subsections.title: Using a Guest Pass
bullets: Guest can receive their guest pass via email with link to web UI
UI shows when the pass is valid for and the customer (who will be issuing the guest pass)
Buttons available for each reader to unlock

subsections.title: Events
bullets: Events in the Elements event feed shows when a guest pass is used and where it was used

caseStudy.title: Flow & Design
paragraphs: {{artifact:InVision flow screenshot}}
{{artifact:Guest pass list}}
{{artifact:Create guest pass}}
{{artifact:Side panels}}
I mapped the flow in InVision Freehand, then moved to hi-fi in Figma using the LenelS2 design system I helped maintain.
bullets: User navigates to the “Guest Passes” area of Elements
User selects the add button to add a guest pass
User inputs a name, activation and expiration dates and times, and the recipient email
User adds readers
User generates the pass
In high fidelity I moved sharing to its own screen so edits do not re-send the pass. Hosts can copy the link through any channel they prefer.

caseStudy.title: Guest-Facing UI & Animation
paragraphs: {{artifact:Guest UI (open animation)}}
{{artifact:Guest UI (error animation)}}
Once creation was designed, I built the guest-facing web UI.
Guest passes live on standalone pages outside the main Elements interface, which allowed animated unlock buttons that confirm the tap registered at the door.
I built an HTML and CSS reference of the unlock animations in CodePen [here](https://codepen.io/JEScarani/pen/oNWKmxG).

caseStudy.title: Conclusion & Results
paragraphs: Guest Pass served two distinct audiences, the organization running Elements and the guest using temporary access.
The project strengthened my ability to map flows in a complex system and use animation to improve perceived responsiveness.
It released in Q4 2021 and is included in sales demonstrations, with ongoing requests for additional functionality.

constraints: Needed to fit within an existing product ecosystem and patterns
Had to support pass issuers and visiting guests as separate user groups
process: Defined users, roles, permissions, and key workflows (issuer + guest)
Mapped end-to-end flow (create pass → share → use → manage/expire)
Created low-fi flow and wireframes (InVision Freehand)
Produced hi-fi designs in Figma using the LenelS2 design system
Designed guest-facing web UI and button animations for clearer feedback
impact: Drove follow-up feature requests from customers

projects.title: JRCS Command Task

heroImage.alt: JRCS Command Task project cover image

projects.problem: Design challenge to warn a ship's bridge of an imminent collision without obscuring other critical navigation information.

caseStudy.title: The Problem
paragraphs: JRCS Digital Innovation Lab develops a command application that gives captains and officers navigation information for their vessel and highlights nearby traffic through AR.
{{artifact:Given screens (start)}}
The team provided two existing screens and asked me to design a collision warning pattern.

caseStudy.title: Users and Requirements
paragraphs: I began by defining the primary users and the requirements for an effective warning experience.

subsections.title: Users
bullets: Captains
Officers on “watch”

subsections.title: Requirements
bullets: Must grab the user's attention
Must provide enough information to act on
Cannot obscure other critical navigation data

caseStudy.title: Sketches
paragraphs: {{artifact:Sketches}}
My first approach was a popover pointing at the vessel on a collision course. After testing three shapes, a rectangular window provided the necessary detail without obscuring the chart.
I also explored projected ship paths and removed that concept because it would be difficult to implement in rough seas and computationally expensive.
Because the application includes a compass-like view, I explored a warning treatment for that context as well.

caseStudy.title: Lo-fi Wireframes
paragraphs: {{artifact:Lo-fi wireframes}}
After sketches, I focused on the primary view and created a couple low-fi variations for the popover.

caseStudy.title: Hi-fi Wireframes and Progression
paragraphs: {{artifact:Hi-fi progression}}
{{artifact:Popover in context}}
After deciding on a structure, I stylized the popover using the existing UI style so it matched the application’s design standards.
From there, I progressively refined the design by adding clearer labels and a boat indicator.

caseStudy.title: Pulse (Attention Mechanism)
paragraphs: {{artifact:Pulse attention bar}}
Drawing on patterns from first-person shooters such as Halo and Call of Duty, I added a pulsing red bar at the top of the display to reach peripheral vision without covering navigation data.

caseStudy.title: Accessibility checks
paragraphs: {{artifact:Transparency comparison}}
{{artifact:Color-blind filters}}
I evaluated legibility across sunrise, sunset, and night backgrounds and tested the design with color-blind simulation filters so red was not the only signal.

caseStudy.title: Conclusion
paragraphs: The team responded positively to the work, although the role ultimately went to another candidate. It remains one of the most engaging problems I have worked on.

constraints: Time-boxed scope with limited domain context
Must grab attention without drowning out critical navigation information
Needed to communicate decisions and trade-offs clearly
process: Clarified goals, users, and requirements from the prompt
Sketched warning concepts and evaluated feasibility trade-offs
Created lo-fi wireframes and compared layout options
Developed hi-fi designs aligned to existing UI standards
Validated legibility across backgrounds and checked accessibility with color-blind filters
impact: Delivered a structured warning concept with clear rationale and trade-offs
Demonstrated prioritization under time constraints and attention to accessibility

projects.title: Vendor-Client Gateway Redesign

heroImage.alt: Vendor-Client Gateway Redesign project cover image

projects.problem: The Vendor Client Gateway is CobbleStone's client-facing add-on for Contract Insights. The experience was outdated, over-configurable, and difficult to use on mobile devices. I led the phase-1 redesign.

caseStudy.title: Overview
paragraphs: The Vendor Client Gateway is an add-on for Contract Insights, CobbleStone's procurement and contract platform.
Clients and support staff had raised concerns for years about a non-responsive layout, outdated UI patterns, and per-client customization that often reduced usability.

During a broader UX initiative across the platform, I led the Gateway redesign with responsive layouts, clearer navigation, UI patterns aligned to Contract Insights, and a narrower set of configuration options.

caseStudy.title: Problem
paragraphs: {{artifact:Before: Home}}
{{artifact:Before: Solicitations}}
{{artifact:Before: News}}
The existing gateway created friction for vendors and limited how useful the module could be.
bullets: Non-responsive layout that was difficult to use on mobile devices
Outdated UI patterns that hurt usability and trust
Over-customization that let clients break their own vendors' experience
Inconsistent workflows around solicitations and contract management

caseStudy.title: Approach
bullets: Audit & evaluation of the existing gateway
Competitive inspiration from similar vendor portals
Design simplification to reduce harmful customization
Iterative design with internal feedback

caseStudy.title: Solution
paragraphs: {{artifact:After: Home}}
{{artifact:After: Solicitations}}
{{artifact:After: News}}
bullets: Responsive layouts across desktop and mobile
Improved navigation and information hierarchy
Standardized UI patterns
Simplified configurations to reduce UX risk

caseStudy.title: Future Plans
paragraphs: Phase 1 of a three-phase roadmap to redesign existing features, expand capabilities, and iterate based on live feedback.

constraints: Non-responsive design made the experience difficult on mobile devices
Outdated UI patterns reduced usability and trust
Over-customization allowed configurations that harmed usability
Inconsistent workflows, especially around solicitations management
Balanced user needs, business goals, and technical constraints in a mature enterprise product
process: Audit and evaluation of the existing gateway to identify usability issues and outdated patterns
Competitive review of similar vendor portals to understand current interaction expectations
Design simplification to reduce harmful customization
impact: Improved mobile usability for vendor workflows
Reduced friction in the module's most common tasks
Established design patterns for the next two roadmap phases
